rows.annotation: The constants $a,b$ are supplied before the input clauses. Hence the exact formula determines the random seed type uniformly for the whole verifier, which is used when the converse enumerates seeds.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is exactly the condition in the fragment: for every $n$, the number of random bits equals $a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+b$.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.CanonicalRandomness
rows.annotation: Once $a,b$ are fixed, the verifier uses a specified number of fair bits at every input length. Lean’s `CanonicalRandomness a b` is the equation `V.randomness n = a * Nat.clog 2 (n + 2) + b` for all `n`. Here `Nat.clog` rounds the logarithm up. The converse uses this equation to generate and enumerate the seeds from the length alone.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is exactly the budget $a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+b$ explained by the table, for every input length $n$.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.CanonicalRandomness
rows.annotation: The budget is fixed at each $n$, even if some runs can ignore part of the seed. The finite seed type still ranges over all bit strings of that length, giving the uniform denominator in `accProb`.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage gives the randomness formula; the formal theorem supplies its fixed constants together with one verifier satisfying all the other resource, time, completeness and soundness requirements.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The exact formula with fixed natural-number coefficients gives the logarithmic part of the PCP claim. It also bounds the number of possible seeds by a polynomial, the quantity needed for deterministic enumeration in the converse.

rows.fidelity_note: The quoted fragment gives a polynomial proof-address bound for every input; the formal theorem supplies that polynomial and all the other verifier guarantees at once.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The polynomial is chosen once for the language and evaluated at each input’s length. It bounds every reachable address even though the tree can depend on the particular input and seed.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is the address-bound condition used here; taking $N=p(|x|)$ gives the displayed polynomial proof bound, required for every input.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.ReadsBelow
rows.plain: Proof-address bound across seeds and branches
rows.annotation: `ReadsBelow` requires all nodes at every seed to have address strictly below $p(|x|)$. This makes agreement on those $p(|x|)$ bits sufficient for identical acceptance on every seed.

ties.name: PCP.Verifier.ReadsBelow
ties.plain: Proof-address bound across seeds and branches

rows.fidelity_note: With $N=p(|x|)$, the formal definition says that every address in every branch lies below the stated polynomial bound, exactly the property explained in the table.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.ReadsBelow
rows.plain: Proof-address bound across seeds and branches
rows.annotation: The address bound uses zero-based indices, so the first $p(|x|)$ bits include every address strictly below that value. No choice of answers can steer a run beyond the prefix.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage gives the polynomial proof-address bound; the formal theorem supplies one polynomial valid for every input together with all the other verifier guarantees.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The theorem places this bound alongside the constant query limit because they govern different quantities. A short execution may reach a far-off address, so the separate polynomial bound makes the proof prefix a polynomial-size witness.

rows.fidelity_note: The quoted fragment gives perfect completeness; the formal theorem supplies it together with soundness, efficiency and the resource bounds for one verifier.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: `V.CompleteAt x` is required whenever `L x` holds. It chooses a proof for that input while the verifier, algorithm and budgets were already fixed for the language.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is the perfect-completeness property in this fragment: a proof accepted with probability $1$ exists at $x$. The fragment requires it for every member of $L$.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.CompleteAt
rows.plain: One proof accepted on every seed
rows.annotation: `CompleteAt` quantifies over proofs before evaluating their acceptance probabilities. One proof must therefore make all seeds accept, and the theorem requires such a choice for every yes-input.

ties.name: PCP.Verifier.CompleteAt
ties.plain: One proof accepted on every seed

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is the property explained in the conclusion: some proof is accepted with probability $1$ at the input. The main theorem requires this property whenever $x\in L$.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.CompleteAt
rows.plain: One proof accepted on every seed
rows.annotation: The probability-one statement is equivalent to universal acceptance over the finite uniform seed type. A single rejecting seed on the proposed proof would lower its acceptance probability.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage gives perfect completeness on members of $L$; the formal theorem supplies it for the same verifier that also has soundness $1/2$, polynomial time and the stated resource bounds.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The completeness clause applies to the same verifier that has the address cap. An accepting oracle for a yes-input can therefore be agreed with on its accessible prefix to obtain a finite accepting witness.

rows.fidelity_note: The quoted fragment gives soundness on nonmembers; the formal theorem supplies it together with perfect completeness, efficiency and the resource bounds.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The premise `¬ L x` activates the soundness bound on a particular input. The same verifier that has perfect completeness on yes-inputs must reject at least half its seeds for every proof on that input.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is the soundness condition in the fragment: every proof has acceptance probability at most $1/2$ at each input outside $L$.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.SoundAt
rows.annotation: For a no-input, pick any proof oracle and freeze it before varying the seed. Its acceptance probability must be at most $1/2$. In Lean, `SoundAt` starts with `∀ π : ProofOracle` and compares `V.accProb x π` with the threshold. As `accProb` counts over the finite uniform seed set, this means at least half its seeds reject for each fixed oracle.

rows.fidelity_note: With $s=1/2$, the formal definition is the universal acceptance bound explained in the conclusion. The main theorem requires it whenever $x\notin L$.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.SoundAt
rows.annotation: This is a bound on acceptance for every individual proof. Neither an honest encoding nor a computable origin for the proof is a premise of `SoundAt`.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage bounds every proof's acceptance by $1/2$ on nonmembers; the formal theorem gives this bound together with perfect completeness and all time and resource guarantees for one verifier.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: A candidate prefix for a no-input can be extended to an arbitrary full oracle and still falls under this clause. It must therefore fail some seed, which is how the converse excludes false witnesses.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement establishes the stated inclusion with perfect completeness and a polynomial-time verifier; it makes the logarithmic budget, fixed query bound, polynomial proof-address bound and soundness $1/2$ explicit.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: `np_subset_pcp` proves the forward inclusion. Its `ReadsBelow` and implementation clauses make the asymptotic resource statement usable in the concrete machine model. Equality of the classes uses the separate converse in Section 5.

topics.description: Polynomial-time verification with logarithmic randomness and a constant number of proof-bit queries characterizes NP.
topics.name: PCP theorem

topics.description: A language belongs to NP when membership is witnessed by a polynomial-length string accepted by a polynomial-time checker.

topics.name: Low-degree extension

topics.description: A polynomial vanishing on a grid admits a decomposition using the coordinate vanishing polynomials and a certificate expressed by two identities.
topics.name: Vanishing certificates

topics.description: Vertex values and edge differences satisfy polynomial equations exactly when they define a proper three-colouring.
topics.name: Colouring constraints

topics.description: Four pairs of points and lines tables supply the answers read by four low-degree tests, two grid tests and a difference check.
topics.name: Proof tables and checks

topics.description: An honest colouring passes every check, while sufficiently small rejection forces four nearby polynomials to describe a proper colouring.
topics.name: Completeness and soundness

topics.description: Corrected certificate queries test vanishing identities at prescribed points and relate failure on the grid to rejection.
topics.name: Zero-on-grid test

topics.description: Random line queries recover a polynomial value at a prescribed point or bound the probability of accepting a wrong value.
topics.name: Local correction over fields

topics.description: Weighted bit queries and tests of encoded line entries recover a homogeneous observation at a prescribed point, allowing rejection.
topics.name: Local correction on bits

topics.description: Small rejection gives one polynomial whose encoding is close to the points table on both full and homogeneous labels.
topics.name: Binary low-degree test

topics.description: A random choice between Hadamard testing and a binary weighted identity tests one encoded line entry for low degree.
topics.name: Inner low-degree test

topics.description: Writing exponents in a fixed number of base digits replaces a line polynomial by a polynomial of fixed total degree.
topics.name: Set-multilinear encoding

topics.description: Agreement with supplied line polynomials at random points yields one nearby polynomial of bounded total degree.
topics.name: Point-versus-line test

topics.description: Weighted interpolation at generator powers tests low degree, with plurality correction turning small rejection into polynomial agreement.

topics.name: Bivariate agreement

topics.name: Hadamard test
